The New York Times filed a lawsuit against Brave Software on 2 November 2026, accusing the privacy‑focused browser of scraping copyrighted articles and providing them to AI firms.
The complaint was joined by the New York Daily News, Chicago Tribune and Orlando Sentinel, which filed similar claims the same day.

The suits allege that Brave’s “Paywall blocker” lets users read articles without publisher consent while the company sells an index of the scraped pages to AI companies such as Anthropic, Perplexity, Mistral, xAI and Cohere.
According to the filings, Brave built an index of more than 30 billion web pages using an undisclosed crawler, a scale that prevents publishers from blocking the collection.
The index is offered to AI developers as “real‑time online content,” enabling models to train on or retrieve news articles for user queries.
The complaint states Brave never asked publishers for permission, nor compensated them for the copying and distribution of their material.

Graham James, a spokesperson for The New York Times, said Brave “stealing our content to power its own products and to provide it to some of the most prominent and well‑resourced generative AI companies in the world”.
Web browsers can crawl and store web pages, creating searchable indexes that third parties may license.
In recent years, AI developers have sought large, up‑to‑date text corpora to improve language models, leading to legal scrutiny of how that data is obtained.
The lawsuits represent a broader push by publishers to protect revenue from paywalls and to enforce copyright against unauthorized data harvesting.

Anthropic added new language to its Risk Factors in a filing on 2 November 2026, warning it may soon meet its own definition of recursive self‑improvement (RSI).
The company says its use of AI to accelerate research could cause model capabilities to grow faster than safety measures can keep up.
It notes past instances where AI‑developed models showed unexpected capability jumps that were not recognized at the time.
The filing states that Anthropic has already used AI to create new models whose capability leaps were missed initially.
It further claims that internal estimates suggest it could imminently reach a threshold of "dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI" as defined in its Responsible Scaling Policy.
Anthropic cautions that such acceleration may outpace its ability to validate, align, and secure the models, posing a considerable safety risk.
Recursive self‑improvement describes a scenario where an AI system becomes capable of improving its own design, leading to rapid capability gains.
While some view RSI as a potential existential threat, others see it as a path to major productivity gains.
Anthropic’s warning reflects broader industry concerns about balancing rapid AI advancement with robust safety and alignment practices.

Apple is developing a home robot that can move around a house, support FaceTime calls and turn lights on when someone enters a room.
The robot, code‑named J595 and possibly called HomeView Ultra, is being pushed by CEO John Ternus and is slated for a launch in 2027 or later.
Apple aims to price the device at $1,000 or more.
The project began with early prototypes in 2018, which received approval from former CEO Tim Cook to continue development.
Apple’s robotic team is small, about ten true roboticists, while the software side includes roughly 300 engineers.
Engineers are adding AI capabilities beyond simple video calls to justify the high price, though current features appear modest compared with existing smart‑home products.
Apple’s HomeView Ultra would join a market of stationary smart displays and robot vacuums, but it differs by being mobile and integrating video communication.
The company also backs another robot effort aimed at tasks like folding clothes, suggesting a longer‑term interest in household robotics.
Safety concerns favor a limited‑purpose robot over a general‑purpose humanoid at this stage.

Oracle filed plans on Monday to issue $10 billion in common stock and $10 billion in senior notes to finance its artificial intelligence buildout.
The filing followed an investor‑day presentation that outlined the fundraising strategy.
Shares fell 8.8% after the announcement despite the company’s earlier revenue forecast of at least $225 billion for fiscal 2030.
The company intends to use the proceeds for general corporate purposes, which may include capital expenditures, debt repayments and future investments.
Oracle expects to achieve positive free cash flow in the second half of 2028 by leveraging vendor financing, customer‑provided hardware and pre‑payments.
Its stock has dropped 33% in 2026 and 50% over the past year, while its investment‑grade 4.95% bond due 2031 yields 7.276%.
Oracle, co‑founded by former CEO Larry Ellison, is expanding its AI infrastructure amid a broader industry push for large‑scale compute resources.

Israeli startup 42AI announced its first product, a behavioral world model, after emerging from stealth with $62.5 million in seed funding on 2 November 2026.
The model is being piloted at a few financial brokerages to forecast how individual traders will react to market volatility.
The company says the system predicts decision probabilities rather than deterministic outcomes.
The model ingests diverse signals such as KYC completion, onboarding interactions, support calls, voice sentiment, and trading activity to infer underlying psychological traits.
Those traits are encoded as mathematical vectors and fed into a transformer‑based world model that outputs probability distributions for future actions.
A separate language model generates natural‑language explanations for each prediction.
42AI’s CEO Amit Gal‑Or emphasizes that behavior is probabilistic, while CTO Ehud Ezra notes the model preserves a person’s risk‑aversion tendency across simulations.
Traditional predictive systems rely on past behavior patterns; 42AI instead attempts to model internal motivations, treating each individual as a miniature world.
This approach aims to improve forecasts in novel situations where historical data may be sparse.
